notes.summary: Nationalism in India traces the national movement from the First World War through the Rowlatt Satyagraha, the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34), showing how different social groups joined with their own idea of swaraj and how a sense of collective belonging was built. CBSE asks dates and leaders, causes and results, why groups joined or stayed away, and chronology and assertion-reason items.
keyPoints: Effects of the First World War: huge defence spending met by war loans and higher taxes (customs duties raised, income tax introduced); prices nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918; forced recruitment in villages; crop failures and an influenza epidemic (12–13 million deaths, Census of 1921).

Gandhi returned from South Africa in January 1915. Early satyagrahas: Champaran 1917 (against the indigo plantation system), Kheda 1917 (peasants seeking revenue relief after crop failure and plague), Ahmedabad 1918 (cotton mill workers).

Rowlatt Act 1919 allowed detention without trial; Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha on 6 April 1919. At Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, on 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi), General Dyer ordered firing on a crowd.

Khilafat Committee formed in Bombay in March 1919 (Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali). The Congress agreed to Non-Cooperation at Calcutta (September 1920) and adopted it at Nagpur (December 1920). In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi argued British rule survived only because Indians cooperated.

Non-Cooperation in towns: boycott of foreign cloth halved imports, value falling from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore (1921–22). It slowed because khadi cost more than mill cloth and alternative Indian institutions were slow to come up.

In the countryside: Awadh peasants under Baba Ramchandra (Oudh Kisan Sabha, October 1920, with Jawaharlal Nehru); Gudem Hills of Andhra under Alluri Sitarama Raju; Assam plantation workers, for whom swaraj meant freedom to move (they were bound by the Inland Emigration Act, 1859).
Chauri Chaura violence (February 1922) led Gandhi to withdraw the movement. C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru then formed the Swaraj Party to return to council politics.
Simon Commission arrived in 1928 and was met with 'Go back Simon'. Lahore Congress, December 1929, under Jawaharlal Nehru demanded Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

Gandhi's letter to Viceroy Irwin (31 January 1930) listed 11 demands, the most stirring being abolition of the salt tax. Salt March: Sabarmati to Dandi, 78 volunteers, about 240 miles in 24 days; salt law broken on 6 April 1930. Gandhi–Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931; Second Round Table Conference in London (1931) failed; Poona Pact, September 1932.

Collective belonging: the image of Bharat Mata (Bankim Chandra's 'Vande Mataram', Abanindranath Tagore's painting), folklore collected by Rabindranath Tagore and Natesa Sastri, and the Swaraj flag of 1921 (red, green and white with a spinning wheel).
traps: Confusing the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22: boycott, surrender of titles, non-cooperation) with the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34: deliberately breaking colonial laws such as the salt law).
Mixing up Champaran (indigo), Kheda (revenue relief) and Ahmedabad (mill workers).
Assuming every group wanted the same swaraj: rich peasants, poor peasants, tribals, plantation workers and businessmen each understood it differently.
Date slips: Lahore session in December 1929 but Independence Day on 26 January 1930; Dandi March began on 12 March but the salt law was broken on 6 April 1930.
Thinking Gandhi supported separate electorates for Dalits: he opposed them and fasted; the Poona Pact gave reserved seats elected by the general electorate instead.
notes.examTip: For chronology and assertion-reason questions, anchor on four points — 1919 (Rowlatt, Jallianwala), 1920 (Non-Cooperation), 1929–30 (Lahore, Dandi) and 1931–32 (Gandhi–Irwin Pact, Poona Pact) — and place every other event relative to them.

questions.text: On 13 April 1919, a crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar was fired upon on the orders of:
options: Lord Irwin
General Dyer
Sir John Simon
Lord Chelmsford
questions.explanation:
After protests against the Rowlatt Act, martial law was imposed in Amritsar and General Dyer took command.
On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi day) he blocked the exits of Jallianwala Bagh and ordered his troops to fire on the crowd, killing hundreds.
He later said his aim was to create terror and awe in the minds of satyagrahis.
So the answer is General Dyer.

questions.text: In Awadh, the peasant movement against talukdars and landlords, who demanded very high rents and begar (forced labour), was led by:
options: Alluri Sitarama Raju
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Baba Ramchandra
Abdul Ghaffar Khan
questions.explanation:
The Awadh peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier gone to Fiji as an indentured labourer.
They demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and social boycott of oppressive landlords.
By October 1920 the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and a few others.
So the answer is Baba Ramchandra.

questions.text: After the Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn, some Congress leaders formed the Swaraj Party to argue for a return to council politics. It was formed by:
options: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru
Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose
Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant
questions.explanation:
Some leaders wanted to contest elections to the provincial councils set up under the Government of India Act of 1919 and oppose British policies from within.
C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress for this purpose.
Younger leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose instead pressed for more radical mass agitation and full independence.
So the answer is C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.

questions.text:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
I. Arrival of the Simon Commission in India
II. Gandhi–Irwin Pact
III. Jallianwala Bagh massacre
IV. Lahore session of the Congress demanding Purna Swaraj
options: I, III, IV, II
III, IV, I, II
IV, III, I, II
III, I, IV, II
questions.explanation:
Jallianwala Bagh massacre: 13 April 1919 (III).
Simon Commission arrived in India: 1928 (I).
Lahore Congress session demanding Purna Swaraj: December 1929 (IV).
Gandhi–Irwin Pact: 5 March 1931 (II).
Correct order: III, I, IV, II.

questions.text: In 1918, Mahatma Gandhi organised a satyagraha movement in Ahmedabad in support of:
options: peasants hit by crop failure who could not pay revenue
cotton mill workers
peasants struggling against the oppressive indigo plantation system
tribal people denied entry into forests
questions.explanation:
Gandhi's three early satyagrahas in India were:
Champaran, Bihar (1917): peasants against the oppressive indigo plantation system.
Kheda, Gujarat (1917): peasants affected by crop failure and a plague epidemic who could not pay revenue.
Ahmedabad (1918): cotton mill workers.
So the 1918 Ahmedabad satyagraha supported cotton mill workers.

questions.text: Why did Mahatma Gandhi choose salt as the symbol for launching the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930?
options: Salt was produced only in England and imported into India
The Congress had asked Indians to stop using salt
Salt was consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and the tax on it showed the most oppressive face of British rule
Salt was India's most valuable export to Britain
questions.explanation:
On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent Viceroy Irwin a letter listing eleven demands; the most stirring was the abolition of the salt tax.
Salt was an essential food item used by everyone, so the salt tax and the government monopoly over its production affected all Indians, rich and poor.
When the demands were not met by 11 March, Gandhi began the Salt March and broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.

questions.text: The Poona Pact of September 1932 between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr B.R. Ambedkar:
options: gave the Depressed Classes separate electorates
gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, to be voted in by the general electorate
abolished untouchability by law
formally ended the Civil Disobedience Movement
questions.explanation:
Dr Ambedkar, who organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930, demanded separate electorates for Dalits at the Second Round Table Conference.
When the British conceded this, Gandhi began a fast unto death, believing separate electorates would slow down their integration into society.
Ambedkar accepted Gandhi's position, and the Poona Pact gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in the provincial and central legislative councils, to be voted in by the general electorate.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): The Non-Cooperation Movement in the cities gradually slowed down.
Reason (R): Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth, and alternative Indian institutions to replace British ones were slow to come up.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation:
The movement in the cities did slow down, so A is true.
Poor people could not afford khadi, so they could not boycott mill cloth for long.
Without enough Indian schools, colleges and courts, students, teachers and lawyers began going back to government institutions.
These are exactly the reasons for the slowdown, so R is true and explains A.

questions.text: Which of the following was NOT an effect of the First World War (1914–18) in India?
options: Customs duties were raised and income tax was introduced to meet defence expenditure
Prices nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918
Forced recruitment of soldiers was carried out in villages
Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced for the first time
questions.explanation:
The war caused a huge rise in defence expenditure, financed by war loans and higher taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax was introduced.
Prices nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918, causing hardship for ordinary people.
Forced recruitment in rural areas caused widespread anger.
Separate electorates for Muslims had been introduced by the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909, before the war, so that was not an effect of the war.

questions.text:
Consider the following statements about the Civil Disobedience Movement:
I. Rich peasant communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh were active participants.
II. Poor peasants joined enthusiastically because the Congress backed no-rent campaigns everywhere.
III. Some industrial workers participated, selectively adopting Gandhian ideas such as the boycott of foreign goods.
IV. Industrialists organised through FICCI (formed in 1927) at first gave financial assistance and refused to buy or sell imported goods.
Which of the statements are correct?
options: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation:
I is correct: rich peasants, hit by falling prices and an unchanged revenue demand, were active supporters.
II is wrong: poor peasants wanted unpaid rent remitted, but the Congress was unwilling to support no-rent campaigns in most places, fearing it would upset rich peasants and landlords.
III is correct: most workers stayed aloof as industrialists came closer to the Congress, but some joined selectively.
IV is correct: business groups supported the movement when it was first launched.
So I, III and IV are correct.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Muslim participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement was as large as in the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat Movement.
Reason (R): After the decline of the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat Movement, a large section of Muslims felt alienated from the Congress, and Hindu–Muslim relations worsened from the mid-1920s.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation:
R is true: after the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation phase, many Muslims felt alienated as the Congress came to be seen as close to Hindu religious nationalist groups like the Hindu Mahasabha, and communal clashes increased.
Because of this, many Muslim political organisations were lukewarm towards the Civil Disobedience Movement and large sections of Muslims did not join it.
So A is false.
Answer: A is false but R is true.
